      "title": "Device limit can deny service to anonymous users and be exhausted by clients",
      "body": "Authenticate fails when TagDevice returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached. The device ID comes from the client-supplied X-Grafana-Device-Id header, so a client can send many unique device IDs until the configured limit is reached; afterwards anonymous requests from new device IDs can be rejected. This turns a tracking/storage limit into an anonymous-access outage. If the limit is meant to cap stored devices, new devices should probably be left untracked but still authenticated; if it is meant to cap access, it needs server-side identity and abuse protection."

      "body": "tagDeviceUI inserts the device key into localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice fails, for example with ErrDeviceLimitReached or a transient database error, the key remains cached for 29 minutes. Subsequent requests for the same device then return nil from the cache, suppressing the original error and treating the device as tagged although no row was written. In the limit case this can make the first request fail but later retries succeed, producing inconsistent enforcement and incorrect device tracking."
    },

      "body": "CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices and, if below the limit, performs a separate upsert. Under concurrent requests, multiple new device IDs can observe count < deviceLimit and then all insert, exceeding the configured limit. If the limit is intended to be hard, enforcement needs an atomic conditional insert, transaction, or database constraint."
    },

      "title": "Anonymous authentication now blocks on device-tag database work",
      "body": "TagDevice was previously invoked asynchronously with its own timeout, but Authenticate now performs it synchronously on the request context. For uncached devices this executes a COUNT query and an upsert before the anonymous identity is returned, adding database latency to anonymous page loads and API calls and making anonymous authentication more sensitive to database slowness."

      "severity": "medium",

      "body": "TagDevice returns nil immediately if X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent, and Anonymous.Authenticate then succeeds. Because the header is optional and client-controlled, a client can avoid the device-limit check entirely by not sending it. If the limit is intended to restrict anonymous devices or sessions, absence of the header should not silently bypass the limit."

findings.title: Device limit can deny service to anonymous users and be exhausted by clients
findings.body: Authenticate fails when TagDevice returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached. The device ID comes from the client-supplied X-Grafana-Device-Id header, so a client can send many unique device IDs until the configured limit is reached; afterwards anonymous requests from new device IDs can be rejected. This turns a tracking/storage limit into an anonymous-access outage. If the limit is meant to cap stored devices, new devices should probably be left untracked but still authenticated; if it is meant to cap access, it needs server-side identity and abuse protection.

findings.title: Local cache is populated before device persistence and not rolled back on error
findings.body: tagDeviceUI inserts the device key into localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice fails, for example with ErrDeviceLimitReached or a transient database error, the key remains cached for 29 minutes. Subsequent requests for the same device then return nil from the cache, suppressing the original error and treating the device as tagged although no row was written. In the limit case this can make the first request fail but later retries succeed, producing inconsistent enforcement and incorrect device tracking.

findings.title: Limit check and insert are not atomic
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices and, if below the limit, performs a separate upsert. Under concurrent requests, multiple new device IDs can observe count < deviceLimit and then all insert, exceeding the configured limit. If the limit is intended to be hard, enforcement needs an atomic conditional insert, transaction, or database constraint.

findings.title: Anonymous authentication now blocks on device-tag database work
findings.body: TagDevice was previously invoked asynchronously with its own timeout, but Authenticate now performs it synchronously on the request context. For uncached devices this executes a COUNT query and an upsert before the anonymous identity is returned, adding database latency to anonymous page loads and API calls and making anonymous authentication more sensitive to database slowness.

findings.title: Device limit is bypassed when the device header is omitted
findings.body: TagDevice returns nil immediately if X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent, and Anonymous.Authenticate then succeeds. Because the header is optional and client-controlled, a client can avoid the device-limit check entirely by not sending it. If the limit is intended to restrict anonymous devices or sessions, absence of the header should not silently bypass the limit.

findings.title: No-limit value is serialized as 0 while frontend expects undefined
findings.body: FrontendSettingsDTO.AnonymousDeviceLimit is a non-pointer int64, so the frontend settings JSON always contains anonymousDeviceLimit: 0 when no limit is configured. The TypeScript type is number | undefined and the runtime default is undefined. Frontend code that distinguishes undefined from 0 may interpret no limit as an explicit zero limit. Use a pointer/omitempty or make the frontend contract explicit that 0 means unlimited.

findings.title: Negative device_limit is silently treated as unlimited
findings.body: AnonymousDeviceLimit is read with MustInt64(0) and the store only enforces values greater than zero. A negative configuration value, likely a typo, is accepted and disables the limit instead of failing validation or being clamped to zero.

findings.title: Device-limit tests do not cover updating an existing device at the limit
findings.body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second new device is rejected when limit=1. It does not verify that an existing active device can still be updated after the limit is reached, nor that stale devices behave as intended. These are the main enforcement paths and should be covered.
